extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics faculty, curriculum designers, and instructors of general-education quantitative reasoning courses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for creating and running a college-level general-education quantitative reasoning / problem solving course (catalog description, goals, placement, curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, and sample activities). Useful to departments designing or revising such courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course goals (Problem Solving)
rubrics_metrics.description: To involve the student directly in various problem solving activities; To contribute to the student’s ability to solve non-routine problems; To expand the student’s methods of inquiry and exploration; To contribute to the student’s ability to form conjectures and check implications; To expand the student’s understanding of major concepts, methods and applications of quantitative reasoning; To help the student see the role of problem solving in modern society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty described a desire to provide a “rigorous but gentle” exposure to quantitative reasoning for students with math anxiety; goals are reflected in syllabus and classroom activities rather than only in lectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalog description (Problem Solving)
rubrics_metrics.description: A general education course whose major goal is to develop the ability to solve non-routine problems through dynamic processes of inquiry and exploration, logical reasoning, making and testing conjectures, and investigating implications of conclusions. A study of major concepts, methods, and applications of quantitative reasoning with emphases on active problem solving and developing connections with other disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course should emphasize active problem solving and interdisciplinary connections; catalog text frames course purpose and expectations for students and advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must have junior class standing (57 semester units or more) and show proficiency in elementary mathematics to register for this course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proficiency can be shown by scoring at or above the 35th percentile on the mathematics portion of the SAT, passing the department’s Mathematics Placement Examination, or by passing a departmental remedial mathematics course. Students who take calculus may waive the course. The course designers note that maturity (junior standing) and some general education background improves student success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent textbook and syllabus across sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Every section follows the same textbook and syllabus. The textbook used is For All Practical Purposes (COMAP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although each instructor focuses on particular chapters (planning/scheduling; graph theory; social choice; apportionment; weighted voting; fair division; consumer finance, etc.), common group exercises, class examples, and shared materials (slides, handouts, exam questions) are used to ensure a common student experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grade distribution / assessment weights
rubrics_metrics.description: Grade components are: Three examinations (45 percent); A cumulative final exam (30 percent); Homework (12 percent); A group project (8 percent); Class participation (5 percent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exams and finals are prepared and graded by each instructor; homework sets have significant intersection across sections; there is a single group project for all sections (groups self-selected, 3–4 students). These weights standardize assessment across multiple instructors/sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group project requirements and expected deliverables
rubrics_metrics.description: One group project for all sections; groups are self-selected and can have three or four students. Project examples include: (1) analyzing the Australian weighted voting system (compute Banzhaf power index; find quotas making smallest state powerless or largest state veto-power; analyze fairness), (2) designing efficient route to unlock all classrooms (scheduling/routing), (3) vehicle routing for deliveries (capacity, addresses, orders, speed limits — find minimum number of trucks and routes), (4) estimating number of Easter eggs to fill a gym (packing and volume approximation), (5) analyzing apportionments under different methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects are expected to require application of course concepts (graph theory, optimization, apportionment indices, packing/approximation), computational work, and interpretation/analysis of results. Group size and shared project across sections enforce collaboration and uniform expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical approach: cooperative and discovery learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Course uses group discussion and teamwork; instructor role is coach rather than lecturer; emphasis on teamwork, cooperation and support rather than isolation and competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course developed using research on how people learn to solve problems (Polya, Schoenfeld) and on cooperative learning; classroom configured to support group work; instructors circulate among groups, ask guiding questions rather than give solutions, and give mini-lectures only as needed. This approach aims to build confidence, persistence, and problem-solving skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity-based instruction with required preparatory reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are expected to read background materials before class; most class time is spent on carefully constructed activities that build on the readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities vary (pair or partner work, individual choices) but typically involve investigations with written analyses including interpretative explanations. Excel is used frequently; activities are designed to complement readings and to foster hands-on data and reasoning experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course topics and activity coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Course organized into three sections: (1) Using numbers, functions and graphs; (2) Reasoning; (3) Statistical thinking. Specific topics include planning and scheduling, graph theory (street networks, traveling salesman), social choice and voting methods, apportionment, weighted voting, fair division, consumer finance, multiple-variable functions, indices/ratings, decision making, inductive/deductive reasoning, measures of center/spread, normal distributions and z-scores, probability, conditional probability, sampling and surveys, and general problem solving techniques. Activities 0–27 correspond to these topics (e.g., Activity 0: Reading Mathematics; Activity 5: Evaluating Websites; Activity 11: Richter Scale and Logarithms; Activity 25: Sampling and sample size).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most activities involve Excel and are performed in a computer classroom; topics and activities are interwoven so students complete an activity and write up analysis for each topic; two activities (reading mathematics and evaluating websites) are emphasized as foundational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment practices: attitudinal and skills assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Program used attitudinal surveys (Q1–Q6) asking students to rate agreement from 1 (Strongly agree) to 5 (Strongly disagree) on items about involvement in problem solving, improved ability to solve problems, methods of exploration, making and checking guesses, understanding of key concepts, and seeing importance of problem solving. The department later disaggregated results by students’ high school mathematics background and began experimenting with skills-based assessment methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attitudinal surveys showed generally positive student responses; faculty note difficulties in designing manageable skills assessments for large enrollments (e.g., 240 students per semester). Disaggregation by prior math experience can reveal differential gains and inform course adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: LinC Quantitative Reasoning student learning objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Quantitative Reasoning course must develop students' facility in: converting conceptual information into problems that can be solved quantitatively; using appropriate techniques for analyzing and solving quantitative problems that lead to the formation of a conclusion; creating and reading pictorial and graphical representations of data and data analysis (including relationships among multiple variables); using appropriate technology as a tool for quantitative analysis; and writing and interpreting results and solutions of problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty must fill out a course review sheet and demonstrate how these student learning objectives will be met and assessed for LinC approval. Courses accepted into the category must show assessment plans indicating levels of achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom physical design to support pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Course is taught in a specially designed room that holds 44 students with tables and swivel chairs arranged so students can turn to form groups of four; there is five feet of floor space between rows to enable instructor mobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Room layout supports frequent group discovery activities (>50% of class time), encourages student interaction, and allows the instructor to circulate and provide targeted coaching, which is reported to increase student willingness to ask questions and take risks.
